utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-02-54-R77.5-T in the case against Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Bruce MacFarlane, appearing as the amicus curiae Prosecutor from Canada. Along with me this afternoon and throughout the proceedings is Lori Ann Wanlin, also from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Karim Khan, Guenal Mettraux, and Arina Koligina on behalf of Ms. Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before beginning with the witness, my computer is not on. Can I get help? Okay. Good morning, Mr. Joinet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And I extend a good morning to you, Mr. Joinet. Yesterday, you outlined your experience in the preparation of and participation in various reports, and it's obvious that you have played an important role in the development of some thinking on a number of different issues in relation to those reports, some of which were with -- many of which were with the United Nations. My understanding is that, and I'd like to get your observation on this, that many of those reports lead to a concrete result, either in whole or in part. They certainly contribute to the thinking in the area. But is it safe to say that those types of reports generally are sometimes adopted, sometimes not adopted?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my own reports are concerned, they have always been adopted. As I mentioned yesterday, the decision-making process is the following: You have recommendations. Either they are rejected or they are adopted. So you recommend to take such and such initiative to appoint -- a body or a tribunal, or to appoint a special rapporteur, and if this recommendation is adopted, given that the recommendation and the consequence of the report are together, the report is tacitly or implicitly adopted, but there is always a decision-making process to decide whether recommendations are adopted or not, and all this is outage a magistrat, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Some of your reports, including perhaps the precursor to this Tribunal, were prepared during the 1990s, and I'm just wondering if you're familiar with some of the developments in this Tribunal since then, since its creation in the early 1990s. For instance, are you familiar with Rule 77 concerning contempt of the Tribunal and its provisions?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of this Rule, but I looked at it the last time that I came here to testify, but because of the court schedule, I could not testify, and the Witness Unit gave me a copy of the Rules of Procedure, and I remember this Rule that talks about contempt of court. So the answer to your question is yes, but I should like to add that as far as contempt of court is concerned and the process of it, I'm not fully aware of it, given that I have no common-law training; and, therefore, I do not know of the way it's dealt with in common law, because we have another concept in France which is "outrage a magistrat."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Subsequent to the development of the Rule, Rule 77, there was established a practice direction on contempt, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I object to this line of questioning. If Mr. MacFarlane could explain how it arises out of examination-in-chief. There was no questions asked whatsoever on Rule 77, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection is overruled. You asked the witness about various laws that govern this area, and Mr. MacFarlane is doing the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, there was, established by the Tribunal, a practice direction on contempt. Are you familiar with that document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have this document with me. If I recollect correctly, I have read parts of this document which looks at the various qualifications that were retained in order to characterize some fact as a contempt of court, but I do not have the document with me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. There have been --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I do not remember seeing it in the various binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: There have been a number of decisions of Chambers, both the Trial Chamber and Appeals Chamber, with respect to contempt, and its elements, and it's shape and its contours, and what needs to be established, and so on. Have you seen any of those decisions? And perhaps I could just mention a few, just to see if that might assist you. A decision called Tadic, T-a-d-i-c; Aleksovski, Brdjanin, B-r-d-j-a-n-i-n; Marijacic; Jovic; Haxhiu? Have you read any of those decisions and looked at the Chamber's comments with respect to the nature of the offence of contempt in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I'm 75 years of age, so I don't have the same memory as you, but I will try to remember. I believe that I read a decision regarding the Tadic case, because when I was chairing the Commission on Administrative Detention, General Tadic referred the case to us, claiming that this Court, and it was the Rules of Procedures that were challenged, led to his detention that was of an arbitrary nature; and we had to work for that six months, because the group is made of five people, it's like a trial chamber, there are some deliberations; so I looked into this case, and this is when I started to look at the way your Tribunal operates. But the case of contempt of court post-dates this other case, but I carried on looking into this case, and this is why I looked into the contempt of court case. But I do not have all the details about the contempt of court case regarding the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "General Tadic referred the case to us," who are the "us"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the group that was set up by the Human Rights Commission. It was a working group on arbitrary detention that I was chairing. There was a Mr. Laytikama [phoen] as well, who then went to the ICTR, and there were five members that had been elected by the Human Rights Commission, and we had been seized, but we rejected the case actually, after careful study. But it might have been some delaying tactics from the interested party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, one of the leading decisions in the area is a case called Jovic, J-o-v-i-c, a decision of the Appeals Chamber in 2007. Do you recall if you had a chance to read that decision?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't really remember the ins and outs of it. The name rings a bell. I think I got to know this name when I was working on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of development since the 1990s, and that's really what I'm focusing on at the moment, I'm wondering if a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada has come to your attention which commented on the authority and the importance of this Tribunal on an international level. And let me read an excerpt from this decision from the Supreme Court of Canada in 2005 to see if you have -- if you're aware of it, if you have any comments in relation to it. The Supreme Court said this in an 8:0 unanimous decision: "Since 1994, a vast body of international jurisprudence has emerged from the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the ICTR. These Tribunals have generated a unique body of authority which cogently reviews the sources, evolution, and application of customary international law. Though the decisions of the ICTY and the ICTR are not binding upon this Court, the expertise of these Tribunals and the authority in respect of customary international law with which they are vested suggest that their findings should not be disregarded lightly by Canadian courts applying domestic legislative provisions." Has that --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps before the question is answered, and with a view to assist counsel on the other side, would Mr. MacFarlane be capable of giving us the reference to the case and the issue to which this statement pertains, in particular whether it relates to the definitions of the crimes, which are the main jurisdiction of this Tribunal, or to any other issue. We'd be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to give the citations? I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honours. The citation for the case is Mugesera, M-u-g-e-s-e-r-a versus Canada, Mugesera versus Canada, and what is referred to, I believe, around the world is the neutral citation is 2005 SCC 40. It's a lengthy decision, but what I've just read is from paragraph 126. The hard copy reference is 2005 2 Supreme Court Reports, page 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what were the issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The issue was -- it was a war crimes case. The issue was the elements of the offence that needed to be established under domestic legislation. The leading case was a case called Finta, F-i-n-t-a, and the Court was asked to reconsider the Finta decision. The Court looked to the decisions of this Tribunal, concluded, in essence, that their own previous decision was wrong, in light of the decisions and the guidance from this Tribunal and the ICTR, and it overruled itself on the issue. The case is available on the internet through the -- it appears that we may be able to e-mail it to counsel very shortly, but it's available on that worldwide linkage of court decisions that spans just about all countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in that case, I would object on the issue of relevance. I happen to be familiar with this particular case, Your Honour, and I'm talking off the top of my head, since we haven't received a copy of that document; but I understand that the passage in question, Your Honour, and the reference that was being made by Mr. MacFarlane pertains to the definition of crime against humanity as given by this Tribunal. And I understand that in that context, the Supreme Court of Canada, indeed, made a reference to the definitions and the evolutions that have occurred in this case. I believe, and I will be corrected by my colleague, that there is no reference whatsoever to any issue of contempt in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could outline the basis upon which I'm posing the question. It's not -- I agree it is not a contempt case. I'm putting it forward on the basis that there have been a number of important developments since the early 1990s which are important to understand post many of the reports that have been referred to yesterday, so I'm advancing the thesis that a lot has happened since the early 1990s that has to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, are you familiar with that decision and that line of thinking from the Supreme Court of Canada and, in essence, the endorsement that that high court gave to the work of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with it, or at least as long as I don't have the possibility to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, again in terms of developments in areas --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In terms of developments, I'm going to draw to your attention a practice direction issued by this Tribunal on the 4th of February, 2008, and copies are now being distributed to Chamber and counsel. I expect that it's well known and well understood by those in the Chamber at the moment, and a version in French is being provided to the witness. This is a practice direction on procedure for the variation of protective measures, pursuant to Rule 75(H) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Tribunal for access to confidential Tribunal material. And, Mr. Joinet, I'd like you to take a few minutes to read through the document, and I have some general questions. I'm not going to ask specific questions about specific parts, but I have a few general questions of you concerning the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreter also get a copy of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please let me know which part of the document I should read, or should I read the entirety of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, do you have a copy for the interpreter? He's asking for one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes. We can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can give him mine. I'll share.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, in response to your question, feel free to read the document as a whole. It's one and a half pages. But probably the most important provision is the first one under the heading "Submission of Applications." But feel free to read the entire document. My questions won't relate to a specific provision but, rather, will be more general.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see any heading called "Submission of Applications," or "Presentation de la Requete" in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It's at the top of page 3 on the English version that I have.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. "Submission of Applications," so "forme de la demande," says the entirety of the paragraph. I ask for your patience, because I will have to read this. I believe it's the last paragraph that is of importance, isn't it, as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Well, let's take it one step at a time. The first paragraph with the number 1 in English reads: "An application submitted pursuant to Rule 75(H) of the Rules by a Judge or Bench in another jurisdiction or parties in another jurisdiction authorised by an appropriate judicial authority to rescind, vary or augment protective measures ordered in proceedings before the Tribunal shall be addressed to the President of the Tribunal ...," and so on. I note in particular that it contemplates an application submitted in another jurisdiction or parties in another jurisdiction authorised by an appropriate judicial authority, and what I'd like you to consider is whether -- well, first of all, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is the first time I see this document, in conditions that are rather precarious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Yesterday, you spoke in terms of victims, and I know that you've written extensively and have views on victims' right to know and the ability to be able to pierce through protective measures. Would this sort of mechanism -- would this sort of provision alleviate some of your concerns?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is, legally speaking, very sharp. If I understand your question correctly, in a more layperson kind of way, your question would be that another jurisdiction, apart from this current Tribunal, could look into a case, or would a jurisdiction other than this Tribunal could deal with this case, or what would be the consequences? In other words, could a victim be tried before a national jurisdiction and then ask for damages before a national jurisdiction? You know, I am just reading a document which is rather complex, from a legal point of view, and, therefore, I'm not quite sure about the question. Could you perhaps ask the question once again? Perhaps I can answer by "yes" or "no," depending on the way you ask the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joinet. In light of the language in the first paragraph, that an application may be made by a party in another jurisdiction, my question is whether -- if a victim is able to make application, for instance, a victim in another jurisdiction, to vary or set aside protective measures that the Tribunal previously imposed, would that alleviate some of your concerns with respect to the ability of a victim to know what happened and the importance of victims knowing what happened?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand your question better now. But when you say that you make a request before another jurisdiction, you mean another international jurisdiction, such as the ICJ, or the ICC; or are you talking about another jurisdiction such as a Canadian or a French court, a national court? This is what is not very clear in the question that you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The question, in particular, that I would ask you to consider is: A victim is engaged in litigation in another jurisdiction, seeks documents from this Tribunal and potentially makes an application, is that sort of -- my question is: Is that sort of mechanism -- is that sort of scheme the sort that might alleviate some of your concerns with respect to the right of the victim to know?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me a second. I will answer your question. We are thinking at the level of principles, isn't it? So in order to meet both criteria, namely, that the victim should know the truth and has a right to know what happened, to find a body, for instance, and so on and so forth, and thereafter or at the same time, they have a right to compensation, or to reparation, these are two distinct rights. If the request before another jurisdiction aims at reducing or rescinding confidentiality measures, in order to obtain information so that this right to know or the right to the truth is met, or if it is to obtain reparation or damages, and if this paragraph 1 allows it, then, of course, that would meet the criteria aiming at obtaining reparation or damages and at having the whole truth, and having also some material reparation. This is the question that I touched upon yesterday, it arises because the practice has changed at the ICC, because you have the “partie civile” concept within the ICC. So the rights of the victim cannot be fulfilled before your Tribunal in terms of damages, but they can be fulfilled to the extent that the ICTY can establish the truth. So it is a moral reparation, but is not a material reparation. And this is why there could be a risk if, before another jurisdiction, such as a national one, the victim could actually try to have their 17 rights upheld, and some questions could be raised regarding classified 18 documentation when dealing with genocide, and there will be a problem, 19 because the victim before a national jurisdiction has a right for their case 20 to be heard. And this is the principle of an impartial and independent court, 21 which means fair, and this victim will not have access to this evidence in order to have their rights upheld before another jurisdiction. Hence the request for confidentiality measures or documents to be set aside in order to obtain reparation. And as things stand, regarding the text that you have put forward, there might be an attempt to solve this issue, but I don't think that this issue is solved by this paragraph. But perhaps I haven't quite understood your question yet. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much for your answer. I think it's probably appropriate for me to move on to the next area, although the next area also deals with the notion of the victim's right to know and the importance of that. And I'm going to refer you to a document that I believe my learned friend put to you. It's in his material. It's a report of the Economic and Social Council of the United Nations, dated the 2nd of October, 1997. It is in the updated 65 ter list, volume 3 of 4, at tab 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's tab 58 and tab 59 of the Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I might need the assistance of my learned friend in linking his various documents, so I'm grateful for the advice from my friend. I recognise that there are different binders and different lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you now, Mr. Joinet?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I direct your attention to paragraph 18 in that document, under the heading "The right to know."

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to say "Right to know." It says "Right to justice," in French, "Le droit a la justice."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I believe the witness might not look at the correct document, because in the booth we have a paragraph stating "Le droit savoir."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: On the English version that I'm looking at, immediately before paragraph 17 is a heading "The right to know," and then there's paragraph 17 and paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It's page 5 in the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: If I could refer you to paragraph 18, and I'll read it, and then we can have a little bit of a discussion on it: "Two series of measures are proposed for this purpose," and the purpose is in relation to the heading "The right to know": "The first is to establish, preferably as soon as possible, extra-judicial commissions of inquiry, on the grounds that unless they are handing down summary justice, which has too often been the case in history, the courts cannot mete out swift punishment to torturers and their masters. The second is aimed at preserving archives relating to human rights violations." You recall this statement? It is a report prepared by you .

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to consider that paragraph against the backdrop of one of your comments yesterday to the effect that international justice is slow, and what I'd ask you to consider is whether or not your views have changed since 1997 in light of two developments that I'd like to draw to your attention and get your comments on. The first is what's referred to often as the Bloody Sunday Inquiry or the Saville Inquiry in the United Kingdom, which was established in 1998, and after 12 years is still not finished. So we have a commission of inquiry in the United Kingdom that has lasted 12 years, and we still don't have a report. Are you familiar with that inquiry in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not really been contacted regarding this. I am not aware of what is happening in the UK about this inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could be a bit more precise. Many people would argue that two of the leading countries, when it comes to commissions of inquiry, in calling them, are the United Kingdom and Canada. Are you familiar with the Air India Inquiry in Canada which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. I happen to know a little bit about the Bloody Sunday Inquiry. I wonder the basis upon which my learned friend states it's not finished. Lord Saville reported some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My basis was the web site of the inquiry, which indicated that the report was expected in early 2010. Whether or not there is an interim report, I don't know, but the material that -- including the web site of the inquiry, suggested that the final report was not in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, are you familiar with the Air India Inquiry in Canada, which has been going on for a number of years?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are thousands of inquiries. I cannot answer about an inquiry regarding, I believe, an air crash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, you're not being asked about thousands of inquiries. You're asked about a specific inquiry. Just limit yourself to that inquiry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want a yes/no answer, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, if I was to suggest to you that at least these two particular inquiries have lasted years and years and years, without a report, would that change your view on the viability of commissions of inquiry, firstly? And, secondly, would it change your view on the potential viability of tribunals such as this to deal with matters more expeditiously than commissions of inquiry?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not believe that my point of view would change or evolve. We had a whole debate about fact-finding commissions, and the main principle which is developed in the report was that justice cannot happen quickly because -- and there would be risks of errors. I've 20 experienced that in my youth. I was born in 1934, and I remember that after 21 the liberation of France, what we called popular justice was -- created 22 atrocious sentences. People were sentenced after a three-day trial, people 23 were executed, so I was very much struck by that. So the question is: 24 How can you really investigate on the spot? You need to investigate, which 25 is what we did with Mazowiecki. And the inquiry with Mr. Mazowiecki was not reliable, judicially speaking. You needed to have another commission that was then put into a new document that could be used by tribunals or jurisdictions, so you need another approach. In our legal system, we call it a quasi jurisdictional system; hence, the idea of the truth and reconciliation commissions, with a difference in some cases. We do not reveal names. It was the case for Argentina, in others, we don't reveal names, it was the case of South Africa, but that is the idea behind those types of jurisdictions. We do not wait for justice to be in a position to go through the various cases, because it takes time; and, therefore, that was the need for these commissions, which has developed extensively. I could go on at length on this, but they also play a role of preparation of the mindset of populations, because what is very important in this issue is that when you look for reconciliation, which is the ultimate goal, reconciliation of various people; but I believe that before reconciliation, which is of a moral nature, you have conciliation, which means that you must make sure that people, at some stage, sit around the table, which is of course a figurative sense, and we have to progress towards bringing the whole truth, and we have to do this together. And this is why those truth and reconciliation commissions work necessarily much faster than courts or tribunals. And I will repeat that I'm not in favour with the slowness of international justice, but my experience, as a magistrate within a supreme court, shows that when you look for the truth within the 25 framework of an investigating magistrate or a tribunal, it takes time, and so 1 there is a complimentarity [as interpreted] that I've experienced in the 2 former Yugoslavia, there was investigation on the ground with Mr. Mazowiecki, and then everything was put together in a more legal or judiciary manner with the Bassiouni Commission, and then institutions such as yours have then followed this up. So it is an entire process, and there is no point in time when justice can be rendered speedily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Just one final question in this area, Mr. Joinet. And accepting my learned friend's point with respect to whether or not the report is actually in or not, the -- as an example, the Bloody Sunday Inquiry in the UK has been around for a number of years, perhaps around a decade. Is that, in your view, acceptable speedy justice for victims?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not feel that whichever victim you speak of, they would be happy with any slowness in the judicial process. It's not satisfactory, it's never satisfactory. But, between the desired ideal, and what is practically possible, international justice is trying to do what is practically possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another area, Mr. Joinet, and I'd like to revisit some of your evidence from yesterday. And at a few points, you spoke about confidential orders, protective measures, and the situation when the information sought to be protected is already out there in the public domain, and I believe that you used the phrase "public domain." Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I quoted a case of espionage, if that's what you are alluding to. There was researcher who was suspected of having given a Soviet agent some secret information. I have said it yesterday, but I can repeat it. I do not want to use up the time of the Court. But we realised that everything had already been published in scientific reviews, so it was in the public domain. This was the example that I quoted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you some questions about the notion of public domain and the point at which something enters into the public domain such that some would argue that the confidentiality has disappeared. So I'd like to pose a series of scenarios to you to obtain your observations, your thoughts, on whether that is sufficient to justify the conclusion that something is in the public domain. So these are the scenarios I'd like to get your thoughts on: Assume for the moment that a tribunal, an international criminal tribunal, has issued an order -- a confidential order for protective measures, and a newspaper in India reports on the contents of the order. Some of the facts they get right, some of the facts they get wrong. In your view, has that entered into the public domain such that confidentiality has disappeared?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the exact French terminology, we do not say that they belong to the public domain, but they have been made public by someone that might be based in India or wherever. The public domain is when a public authority will make something public. It could be through a press release from a ministry; whereas here, it is actually a leak, so it is made public. This is a nuance that I have in the French language that may not exist in the English language, but the result is the same, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Is it relevant, in your view, of the fact that the newspapers got some of their facts right and some of their facts wrong?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the English word for "pertinence" that was used? It was "relevant" in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: "Relevance," "pertinent."

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: So is that "relevant"? If they are true facts and full facts, well, then, the author of this article is not a good professional journalist. What else can I say? It is his problem or her problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Does that affect the conclusion as to whether or not the protective measures in the order have been affected? Does that -- is there any relevance assigned to the fact that the newspaper got it right and got it wrong in assessing whether or not confidentiality has been affected?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the journalist has made public some information, whether it is false or true, confidentiality doesn't exist anymore, if that is the sense or the purpose of your question. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So just to clarify, then, your view would be if a single newspaper in a faraway country reported on the protective measures order and got some of the facts right and some of the facts wrong, that confidentiality has disappeared?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a prima facie manner, I would say, yes, something that was made public is no longer confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Would that affect the order itself? That is to say, would the reporting in India, rightly and wrongly, affect the fact that the order was issued confidentially, or does the order remain fully in place to protect the information? 4 A. Given my legal background, I do make a distinction between the container 5 and the content, and the order cannot be considered as confidential. An order 6 for confidentiality cannot be confidential. Otherwise, we are talking about 7 secrecy in justice. What has to remain confidential is the documents to which 8 this order is attached and for which this order has been issued. This is the 9 example that I gave. In France when you decide to have a private session 10 or a closed session, the decision has to be made in open session, and has to 11 be reasoned. The same applies here when you have an order for confidentiality 12 of documents, this order has to be public and reasoned. But once this order 13 has been made public, the evidence, the facts and in the present case, 14 the Serbian documents, which are covered by the confidentiality nature, 15 but not the order itself, in my legal background, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In a situation where a journalist has decided to write with respect to a confidential order, and, for instance, writes a newspaper article, or a book, or something of that sort, who is the one that decides whether that act, by itself, has affected the order, and the confidential nature of the order, and the protective nature of that order? Who decides that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my legal system, in such a situation the prosecutor may or may not initiate proceedings. It is not the tribunal that does it. You cannot be a tribunal and a prosecutor at the same time, so the tribunal cannot decide whether charges will be brought. I'm talking about the tribunal that issued this order. So in my own legal system, the prosecutor will feel that there has been a violation, and in that case, they will contact the relevant jurisdiction for this contempt of court case. That doesn't exist in my system, so it would be a violation of the secrecy of the investigation process, but the approach is the same. So to your question, who will take the initiative, it will be actually the prosecutor's office, not the tribunal, as it would then be both judge and party to the case, and then the tribunal decides whether to confirm charges or not. So I believe that was the question that you asked me. Is the answer what you were expecting from me? I'm not quite sure I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can approach it this way: Can the journalist unilaterally make the decision that an order is no longer confidential or does that decision rest with the tribunal, with the court that issued the order?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the job of a journalist is to produce information, especially when dealing with investigative journalism, so this is their core business. Now, in order to know whether they were releasing classified information, it will be up to the prosecutor's office to see whether a violation was committed. And if that is the case, in my country they will refer this to the tribunal in order for a proceedings to be launched against this journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So that the final determination and the decision results -- or falls to judicial hands?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: It falls to judicial hands in my system, so you will have the tribunal of first instance, then you will have the Court of Appeal, and then you will have the Court of Cessation, so the court of last appeal, and then you will have the European Court of Human Rights, if required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So, in other words, because it false to judicial hands, you can't have a situation where a journalist is saying, Well, I'm going to make the decision that is no longer confidential? It doesn't fall to the journalist, it falls to judicial hands?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the journalist will not make any decision. The journalist will gather some information, and what happens, usually, and it is actually quite frequent, journalists produce information that are covered by a "top secret" seal. We have a newspaper in France called "Le Canard Enchaine," and their main job is to do that, so to say. But it is not up to the journalist to decide. The journalist carries out his/her professional duties, and takes some risks, but it is up to the competent court. If the prosecutor’s office thinks there are grounds to institute proceedings, they will do it. But it is not up to the journalist or the tribunal. And if the prosecutor does not refer the case to the tribunal, the tribunal cannot decide on its own to take the case. Otherwise, the tribunal would be both the judge and the party in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In other words, as I understand what you're saying, if a journalist decides to take the risk, to use your word, to take the risk, the matter could be referred to the prosecutor's office and then to the judicial authorities for a decision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be sent to the prosecutor's office. And it will be up to the prosecutor to take initiative proprio motu. This is what we call the principle of discretionary prosecution, and this is the remit of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'll move on to the next point, and I'd like to refer to a couple of reports that were drawn to your attention yesterday. The first was referred to as item number 79 in the Defence binder. It's a joint declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By "item," you mean "tab"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, "tab," that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will not object to the document, in view of your earlier rulings. We'll simply indicate for the record that this document was not used as shown to Mr. Joinet in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it's a bundle you provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's a bundle you provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and it's in tab 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just lay the foundation while the document is being sought, for the benefit of the witness. This is a document forming part of the Defence documents. It's headed "International Mechanisms for Promoting Freedom of Expression," a joint declaration by the UN special rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression, the OSCE representative on freedom in the media and the OAS special rapporteur on freedom of expression. So there has been UN involvement through the UN special rapporteur on freedom of information and expression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a copy in French?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I don't believe there is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I read everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I will read to you what I believe to be the relevant parts, with a view to assisting you. The heading is a "Joint Declaration," as I mentioned a moment ago, involving the UN special rapporteur and two others having met in London in December of 2002, under the auspices of Article 19, "Global Campaign for Free Expression." And I'd like to draw to your attention the bottom of page 1, under the heading "Freedom of expression and the administration of justice." And there are a series of bullet points under that heading of "Freedom of expression and the administration of justice." The first one I'll read to you, and it will be translated for you: "Special restrictions on commenting on courts and judges cannot be justified. The judiciary play a key public role and, as such, must be subject to open public scrutiny." That's the broad, general statement. The next bullet point at the top of page 2 is the one that I'll be asking you -- actually, the next two I'll be asking you questions about. The one at the top of page 2 reads: "No restrictions on reporting on ongoing legal proceedings may be justified unless there is a substantial risk of serious prejudice to the fairness of those proceedings and the threat to the right to a fair trial or to the presumption of innocence outweighs the harm to freedom of expression."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So just pausing on that one for the moment, "no restrictions on reporting on ongoing legal proceedings may be justified unless ..." and then there are exceptions put forward, "series prejudice to the fairness of those proceedings," "threat to a fair trial," and so on, you would agree, I assume, that while the emphasis in this document, in the joint declaration, is that there should be no restrictions on reporting on ongoing proceedings, there are exceptions. Even under the joint declaration, there are recognised exceptions to that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is another way of saying what I believe I said yesterday. The first paragraph states that when dealing with freedom of expression, freedom should be the rule. And restrictions are admissible, but that should be the exception, and any exception needs to have a strict interpretation, and the grounds that are given would be that when there is a violation of the right to a fair trial or a threat to the presumption of innocence. So this is where the difficulty lies. If you have a restriction that would stop you from having access to some evidence, could we consider that this restriction will constitute a threat to the right of a fair trial? I believe so. If some evidence are not made known, how will the trial be fair? Because some parties will have the evidence, such as a country involved in the case, but not 25 the victim. And as for the presumption of innocence and the threat thereof, I remember that when I testified in a trial against Argentinean generals, of course there was the issue of not communicating some information that remained classified, but while giving this information, there was no threat to the presumption of innocence. Otherwise, justice cannot be rendered. So it is very important to underscore, as Mr. Ligabo said, that they have really pointed out that the rule is freedom, the exception is restriction, and they are strict interpretations. So restrictions can only apply in two cases: violation of the right to a fair trial, and the presumption of innocence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to the next bullet point immediately below that which deals with sanctions that might be applied as a result of legal proceedings, and it reads: "Any sanctions for reporting on legal proceedings should be applied only after a fair and public hearing by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal; the practice of summary justice being applied in cases involving criticism of judicial proceedings is unacceptable." And after you've had an opportunity to read that and consider that, my question is this: Does it not, even in a joint declaration with respect to freedom of opinion and expression -- is it not clear that even within that framework, a sanction is contemplated for reporting on legal proceedings in appropriate circumstances?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are saying -- I'm just reading this in English again. The sanction that is mentioned in this paragraph, it will be a sanction that would be made against a journalist that would have made something public. Is that what this sanction is about in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be a journalist. Anybody who reports on the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that if they are subjected to legal proceedings, it's what we said earlier on, the difficulty - and that's what we mentioned yesterday - is to know whether there is sufficient proportionality between the legal proceedings and the facts that are the subject of those legal proceedings. This is always the principle of international law. A waiver is admissible or an exception is admissible providing it is proportional to the goal, that’s the point, and it's the role of the judges to assess the proportionality nature of the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'd like to move to what I believe is the next document in, I believe, it's tab 80 again in the Defence materials. It's headed "Council of Europe, Committee of Ministers," a declaration. That should be tab 80. I don't believe that we have a French version, so I'll -- oh, we do, we do. 81 is the French version. And what I'll be drawing to your attention, Mr. Joinet, is on page 2, just so you know, under the heading in English "Calls on Member States." So there is a series of preambles in the declaration, and then after the preambles, the declaration calls on member states to do certain things. And I'd like to direct your attention to the very first item that the ministers called on members states to do. Could you read that first one, please?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Calls on member states to encourage responsible reporting on criminal proceedings." Is that what you would like me to read? Okay, I'll ask you for a couple of minutes. Thanks. I have finished reading this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. The paragraph provides that ministers called on member states to encourage responsible reporting on criminal proceedings in the media by supporting the training of journalists in the field of law and court procedure, in cooperation with the media and their professional organisations, and so on. What I'd like you to consider is the opening words, "To encourage responsible reporting on criminal proceedings in the media," and my question to you is this: Is it responsible, on the part of a reporter, in the context that we're talking about, to write about and disclose confidential information?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: The French version of this paragraph deals with an issue that I'm very well aware of. What we are asking the member states is to encourage good training of journalists. Why? Because we have noticed in several countries, including in mine, that the general public has difficulties to understand how justice is rendered, how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, we don't have much time. The question is not about education. The question is: Is it responsible? You are being asked about the first part of that paragraph, not the latter part. Could you please try to stay on to the question. Listen to the question carefully, and please answer the question as directly and succinctly as you possibly can. Maybe Mr. Prosecutor can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the question deals with a text that I've been asked to read, the answer is, yes, one has to be responsible when we are reporting on justice to help the general public to better understand and to make sure that the interests of the various parties are captured. This is the answer that goes without saying, once you have read this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could reframe it slightly to be more precise. Ministers called on member states to encourage responsible reporting on criminal proceedings. My question is: Is it responsible, on the part of a journalist, to write in the media about information which is confidential?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be a male or female journalist, but if the role of a journalist is to write about something, it is up to the prosecutor's office to institute proceedings, if they feel there has been a violation. I go back to this same issue again and again, but this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, yes, we have dealt with whether the prosecution will initiate proceedings. The question is -- you are being asked a question specifically. Is it responsible for a journalist to report about confidential material in legal proceedings? That's a very simple question. It really doesn't need you to go all over the shore. You can answer, yes, it is response; no, it is not responsible; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to answer in a very binary fashion to a complex question, I believe, yes, it is the role of a journalist to seek information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's not the question. The question is: Is it responsible to report on a confidential matter? The question is not: What is the role of the journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The journalist should not feel that they are responsible or not. It is up to the jurisdiction in question to decide whether they are responsible or not. If the journalist feels that they are bound by everything that is confidential, there would be a limitation to the role of the press in such a way that a lot of world events could not be reported by the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the point is, since yesterday you've been testifying here and telling us how much you have written around this area and how much you know about this area. The question has just been put to you, putting aside the judiciary: Do you consider it responsible to do so, given all the knowledge that you have and that you've been testifying to for the last two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I were a journalist, I would say, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not as a journalist. You, as you are, sitting there, as you are, is it responsible or is it not responsible to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I have to answer as if I wasn't in the situation of a journalist? I would tend to say that it is responsible, but it depends as to whether you're a journalist, an attorney-at-law, or an investigating magistrate. There is no yes/no answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Supposing you are Louis Joinet. Would Louis Joinet regard it as responsible or not responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Responsible, as in feeling that I feel the obligation of doing so? I think I would, provided that I'm in a situation when the severity of the facts is such that it is my duty to reveal those facts. And then, if one feels that I went beyond my call of duty, then the legal authorities will instigate some proceedings. But otherwise it would be self-censorship, and this is something that is very important because it is at the core of those jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, I don't have a whole lot of questions left; I do have a few. And the first area deals with some of the -- or one of the documents that was put to you by my learned friend yesterday. It's in the current -- I'll call it the current Mr. Joinet binder that was used yesterday, and it's tab 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The French is at 55, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The French will be 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Just for a little bit of context, this was the Economic and Social Council report tended by my learned friend, dated 1991, and the heading was "Review of further developments in fields with which the subcommission has been concerned," specifically the right to freedom of opinion and expression. And I draw to your attention paragraph - actually, two paragraphs that my learned friend drew to your attention, paragraphs 25 and 26, under the heading of "The question of contempt of court." Do you have paragraph 25 in front of you, Mr. Joinet?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you recall that my learned friend read a portion of this paragraph, but I think it's important that the full paragraph be read. And in English, it reads: "Another member suggested that the rapporteur should go thoroughly into the question of contempt of court in order to think about a restrictive interpretation of that concept. In view of its scope, as a measure restrictive of freedom, it was feared that it might come into unduly common use in the courts." And my learned friend read that part to you, but the next sentence is important, and I'd like to get some background from you. The next sentence, the final sentence says: "There again was not time to go into the matter." Could you tell us a little bit about what that sentence meant?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence, and I think I have a good memory on this matter because there were a lot of discussions, and we consulted colleagues from the subcommission before we drafted the report that you just mentioned, the reason it took quite a while, to start with, is that we wanted to capture what it meant in both legal systems, so common law and civil law. We wanted to try and understand what were the differences and what were the common points between contempt of court and the French concept of "outrage a magistrat," which is the other concept, because we felt that it would be difficult to move ahead on this issue without having a very good knowledge of both legal backgrounds. And they have the same objective, but they have different approaches, as you're aware. The concept of contempt of court is more wide ranging, if I recollect correctly, compared to the concept of "outrage" in French. But the question that was raised yesterday, and I mentioned this yesterday already, was to know whether the legal consequences were the same, whether what is captured in contempt of court happened while the matter was ongoing or pending, namely, while there hadn't been any final determination, death of the accused or statute of limitations. So we felt that if we are within a period where justice has not been fully administered or rendered, there would be a difference compared to a case where the case has terminated by a final judgment, death or the statute of limitation. And in the common-law system, the contempt of court exists in order to prevent interference with the administration of justice. In France, it is more "ad hominem" which means that it is the magistrate that is targeted, whereas contempt of court is more dealing with jurisdiction and the administering of justice in general. And the debate that we had is that if the facts in question happen before the matter is closed, the administration of justice is put in question, but once the matter is concluded or is closed, the administration of justice, by statutes of limitations, or by death, or by decision, has fulfilled its duties; and, therefore, the contempt of court is not as important once the matter is closed as if it was during the administration of justice. So this took us a lot of time, of course, because we had to discuss this in plenary session, and we did not have the time in plenary session to discuss all this, and we decided to leave it there. We contemplated to appoint an ad hoc rapporteur to go more in depth on this issue, but in the end, it didn't happen because the subcommission changed in its composition, and so it did not happen. So that explains this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. So when, at the end of that paragraph, it says that there again was -- there is not time to go into the matter, that was a signal that the views expressed here were preliminary views, that there wasn't that time for a fulsome discussion?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: With respect to paragraph number 26, a similar point. Yesterday, a portion of this was dealt with. The paragraph reads: "The desire was expressed that more specific attention should be paid to the protection of journalists (whether or not on mission), among other measures by appointing a special rapporteur." But the portion that was not dealt with yesterday and which I would ask you to comment on is the next sentence: "It is too early for anything to be said on the subject in the present report ..." Is this essentially the same thing, that it was simply too early to have a fulsome discussion and to arrive at any clear conclusions?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely what it means. It doesn't mean that no initiative was taken thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Joinet, at one point yesterday in your testimony, you made a comment to the effect that -- you made an observation with respect to the objectives of the sentencing process, and you mentioned that the sentencing process was intended and was effective in two ways; firstly, with respect to punishment, and, secondly, with respect to prevention. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking about the role of international jurisdiction, I talked about a sanction and the role of prevention within the framework of international jurisdiction, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: But the point that I'm leading up to is that, in terms of a sentencing process, you saw two dimensions to it, two objectives. One is punishment, but the second is prevention in the future .

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. MacFarlane wished to put this as the proposition of the witness, it would be grateful that he indicate the page of the transcript which he refers, because we have no memory of Mr. Joinet giving evidence on the issue of sentencing. The issue that he talked about was, indeed, the one that he's mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, I'm not sure what was mentioned a moment ago that Mr. Mettraux felt -- and, Mr. Mettraux, the witness himself said: "When talking about the role of international jurisdiction, I talked about the sanction and the role of prevention within the framework of international ...," so the witness does remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, the matter that was raised and the questions that was answered in relation to that, as we understand, was the role -- what was the role of the tribunal, and he mentioned that he could see two roles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the witness does remember. He can clearly -- Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If Your Honour please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, would be fair to say that in your view, the sentencing process does have those two elements or objectives; that is, punishment and prevention?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is, yes. Prevention will be all the more effective if we have a sentencing process as well, if someone is found guilty, of course. And I remember talking about it, because I gave an example which happened during a meeting the prime minister that attended too. There was the chief of staff, upon returning from a trip in the Caucasus and the Balkans, said that the military chiefs are starting to take this seriously, and they are starting to realise that they are running some risks. So I have already touched upon this issue, and I remember that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the sake of the record, in terms of the reference, we've just done an electronic search, which is so handy, and I refer to the bottom of page 287 and the top of page 288 as the points of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Now, the two-prong objectives that you've spoken about, Mr. Joinet, I take it that they ought to apply to all forms of alleged criminal conduct, including contempt of court.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has to do with prevention? Yes. And, again, we must uphold the proportionality principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in a contempt of court context, that prevention is important because it sends a signal to other future writers and authors?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in a contempt of court context, that prevention is important because it sends a signal to other future writers and authors?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be relevant, indeed, but the question is to know whether the credibility of the court or the tribunal was in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, my question doesn't relate to the credibility of the tribunal, but rather to the sentencing process. And my suggestion to you, and I'd like your comment on it, is that as part of the sentencing in a particular case, and given the prevention aspect, that sentencing can act as an important message or signal to future authors who might consider taking a risk in the future.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can go both ways. It can be an important signal for other people that would like to act in this regard, but it could also have some devastating effects on the credibility of a given jurisdiction. Every case is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, if I might have just 30 seconds to check my notes, I think I'm concluded, but ... Thank you, Your Honours. That concludes my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. MacFarlane. Any re-examination, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Joinet. I have a few questions in re-examination for you. And because we're pressed by time, I'll ask you, to the extent you can, to answer as shortly as you can. And if you feel able to do so, to answer with "yes" or "no." Do you recall yesterday, at page 91 and 94 to 95, the Prosecutor asked you a few questions about conflicts of rights? Do you remember him asking you about that? Mr. Joinet, don't concern yourself with the transcript. Just focus on my question. Do you recall the questions about conflicts of rights by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that was at the beginning of his line of questioning. This was a question that I hadn't really grasped very clearly at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you also recall questions being asked about the importance of courts to be able to enforce their orders? Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall also -- and, Your Honour, for the record, it was page 95. Do you recall also being asked questions about the permissible limitations to the principle of freedom of expressions? Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was "admissible" in French for "permissible" in English. There is a nuance in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall being asked specifically about the principle of proportionality and how it applies in the context of freedom of expression? Do you recall these questions?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; very well, actually. This is a core issue to this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall earlier today being asked to comment about various decisions from various jurisdictions? Do you recall those questions? Canada, Great Britain and so on, do you recall those?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that the question was asked, and I was not in a position to reply to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall also being asked a question about information that was in the public domain and the significance of that fact? Do you recall these questions of this morning?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the usher, there's a short bundle of four documents which we would like distributed to the Court, the Prosecutor, and to Mr. Joinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, so that you can familiarise yourself with the document, they are four decisions. I've put them in English and in French so everyone will follow. As you'll see, number 2 and 4 are the versions in French, and I will ask you first to turn to tab 2 of that document. That would be tab 1, Your Honours, in the English. And for the record, Mr. Joinet, this is a case from the European Court of Human Rights. It's the case of Mr. Weber versus Switzerland. It's a judgement of the 22nd of May of 1990. And as I indicated, it comes from the ECHR. Mr. Joinet, with your assistance, could you turn, please, to paragraph 7 of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpreters do not have the set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, could copies of this document be given to the interpreters, please. And I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, do you have paragraph 7 of that decision in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have the correct documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 7, you will see that Mr. Weber is a Swiss journalist that comes from my part of the world in the Canton de Vaud. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to paragraph 13 of that same decision?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Here, I'll ask you specifically to note the date that is mentioned in that paragraph. It says that on the 2nd of March of 1982, Mr. Weber took part at the press conference at which a number of facts that pertain to an ongoing criminal investigations were disclosed. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you look at the next paragraph in that document, you'll see it's paragraph 14, it says that on the next day, the 3rd of March of 1982, a Swiss newspaper, "La Gazette de Lausanne," reported what the applicant had said. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you move onward to paragraph 15 of that document, you will see that following this disclosure of confidential judicial information, a criminal investigation for breach of confidentiality -- a judicial investigation was started. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The next paragraph in the judgement, and I'll just ask you to take my word for it, and if there's any dispute about that, Mr. MacFarlane can perhaps raise it, but the rest of the passage is mentioned, the fact that Mr. Weber was prosecuted in Switzerland and was convicted for his actions. Now, can I ask you to go to paragraph 49 of that document. Perhaps I'll give you a few seconds, Mr. Joinet, to read that paragraph. But may I put it to you, and you can tell me whether you agree or disagree afterwards, that the argument that Mr. Weber raised before the European Court of Human Rights in that particular case was effectively to say that the information which he disclosed was of public knowledge or in the public domain and that the criminal conviction that was imposed on him in Switzerland constituted a violation of his freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention. Can you tell me whether that generally meets what Mr. Weber is suggesting here?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially Article 10, yes, which I'm very well aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you look now at the next paragraph, those are the submissions of the respondent, the Swiss government, and I will read to you what the Swiss government said in response to what Mr. Weber was saying. They said this: "In the government's submission, this finding was not decisive because of the formal nature of the confidentiality referred to in Article 184 and 185 of the Code. According to the relevant Swiss case law and legal literature, the mere fact of communicating a piece of information in a judicial investigation was sufficient for the commission of the offence, whether it was common knowledge beforehand, and its importance or degree of confidentiality were relevant only in determining the amount of the fine." Do you see that submission of the Swiss government?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes. It's the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll ask you to turn to the next paragraph, paragraph 51 of this document, and it's the finding of the Court, of the European Court of Human Rights on that case, and it says this -- talking about the submission of the Swiss government, the Court said this: "The Court finds this submission unpersuasive. For the purposes of the Convention, the interest in maintaining the confidentiality of the aforementioned facts no longer existed on 2nd March 1982." And you will recall that this date, Mr. Joinet, is the date at which the press conference took place. And it goes on to say: "On that date, therefore, the penalty imposed on the applicant no longer appeared necessary in order to achieve the legitimate aim pursued." And if you can now turn to paragraph 52, which is the ultimate finding the Court is making on Article 10, it says: "Having regard to the particular circumstances of the case, the Court concludes that in being convicted and sentenced to a fine, Mr. Weber was subjected to an interference with the exercise of his right to freedom of expression which was not 'necessary in a democratic society' for achieving the legitimate aim pursued." Now, Mr. Joinet, can you tell me whether that's an example or an illustration of a court of law applying the principle of proportionality in the context of freedom of expression and the breach of judicial confidentiality? Is that one example?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it's a very clinical case, because it says that before that date, the principle of proportionality was relevant. But from the 2nd of March, given that the facts were made public, there would not be any question of proportionality, and this is the very reason why paragraph 52 states that it is no longer necessary in a democratic society. Before it was; after that, it is no longer relevant. It is a very clinical case, so to say, of the fundamental role of the proportionality principle, especially when dealing with restrictions within the scope of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Now, do you recall being asked questions by the Prosecutor as to whether you were aware of some changes in international law that the Prosecutor suggested to you had occurred since 1991, when you published your report on freedom of expression. Do you recall those questions of my friend?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't always capture the context, but I remember that they were asked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I would like to show you a recent decision on that point, and that's dated the 12th of November of 2007. And you can find it in the bundle in front of you under tab 4, for the French version, and tab 3 for the English. Again, Mr. Joinet, this is a judgement from the European Court of Human Rights. It's the case of Mr. Dupuis and others versus France, and it's dated the 7th of June of 2007. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps, as a matter of general background - I think there's no dispute about that - this is a case that concerns two journalists, Mr. Dupuis and Mr. Pontaut, who published a book called "Les Oreilles du President." Are you familiar with this book, Mr. Joinet?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that what this book is about is a book written by two French journalists who conducted an investigation of a civilians programme orchestrated by the then French President, Mr. Mitterrand, and which they wrote about in their book? Is that more or less the background of this case?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps to expedite things, and if you're familiar with it, is it correct that as part of this case, or if you know, that these two journalists were charged by the French authorities for revealing the content of documents which formed part of a confidential judicial investigation? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you also familiar with the fact that after they had been charged with an offence under French law, they were convicted by French courts, are you familiar with that, and that their argument based on their freedom of expression was rejected? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can recollect this.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to turn to paragraph 36 of the judgement that you have in front of you, 36. The Court, in its legal consideration, says this: "As a matter of general principle, the necessity 'for any restriction on freedom of expression must be convincingly established.'" And then it goes on to say: "Admittedly, it is in the first place for the national authorities to assess whether there is 'pressing social need for the restriction' and in making their assessment, they enjoy a certain margin of appreciation." Can you see that?
