utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need a couple of minutes. Let me read this out. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then the Court went on to say this: "In the present context of the press, the national margin of appreciation is circumscribed by the interest of democratic society in ensuring and maintaining a free press. Similarly, that interest will weigh heavily --"

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thirty-six, Mr. Joinet.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then the courts goes on to say: "Similarly, that interest will weigh heavily in the balance in determining, as must be done under paragraph 2 of Article 10, whether the restriction was proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued." Let me stop here for a second, Mr. Joinet. Is this definition or description consistent with your understanding of the principle of proportionality, as you referred to following the question of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, all the more that I was actually called as a witness during this trial in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that information, Mr. Joinet. I wasn't aware of it. Can I ask you to turn to paragraph 39 of that document. As you will see, it's the beginning of the section where the Court has applied the law to the facts, if you want, the application to the case. And in the first sentence of paragraph 39, the Court said this: "The Court observes at the outset that the subject of the book was an issue of considerable public interest." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then there's a second consideration at paragraph 40 which the Court applies to its factual consideration. It's the first sentence again, and the Court says this: "The Court reiterates that Article 10(2) of the Convention leaves little scope for restrictions on freedom of expression in the area of political speech or in matters of public interest." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can look at another consideration to which the Court turns its mind, it's at paragraph 41, the first sentence, the Court says this: "Not only does the press have the task of imparting such information and ideas; the public also has a right to receive them." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then in the same paragraph, the Court refers to what it called the considerable degree of emotion pertaining to this issue. And then if you can turn to paragraph 42, it's the next consideration which the Court took into account in this context to apply the law to the fact. Can you see that the Court is referring to the importance of the media role in the area of criminal justice is very widely recognised? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And at the last paragraph, reiterating to some extent the same point, the Court said that: "The public must be able to receive information about the activities of judicial authorities and police services through the media and that journalists must, therefore, be able to report freely on the functioning of the criminal justice system." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the fifth consideration which the Court took into account in the context of its judgement is at paragraph 43, where the Court says that: "Those who exercise freedom of expression, including journalists, undertake 'duties and responsibilities' the scope of which depends on their situation and the technical means they use." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not quite sure where it is. It is 43, paragraph 43? Is it at the beginning of paragraph 43?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It's paragraph 43, and it's the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then I'll give you a second --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Read through paragraph 44, but would it be correct that the other -- one other consideration that the Chamber -- that the Court in this case took into account to apply the principle of proportionality and the necessity of curtailment of the right is the very wide media coverage that was going on about this case, and also the fact, and I quote: " ... that the case was already publicly known that G.M.," that's one of the persons involved in the information provided by the journalist, "had been placed under investigation"? So, I'll give you a few second to read that and ask you whether that's the case or not.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I see very well what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Joinet, that one of the consideration of the European Court of Human Right in that context was, in fact, the very wide media coverage of the case in question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the very last sentence in that paragraph, Mr. Joinet? It says this: "In those circumstances, the protection of the information on account of its confidentiality did not constitute an overriding requirement." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and we could actually say there's "no longer constitute."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then you'll see there's another finding of the Court in the context of the application of this principle in this context. It says this, and it's paragraph 45, Mr. Joinet: "In this connection, it is noteworthy that, while the applicant's conviction for the offence of handling was based on the reproduction and use in their book of documents which had come from the investigation file and which, accordingly, were found to have been communicated in breach of the secrecy of the judicial investigation or in breach of professional confidence, that conviction inevitably concerned the disclosure of information." And it goes on to say: "It is open to question, however, whether there was still any need to prevent disclosure of information that was already at least partly available to the public." Can you see that? And they go on to cite a few cases. And then --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm actually aware of some of those cases that are quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: " ... and might already have been known to a large number of people, having regard to the media coverage of the case, on accounts of the facts and the celebrity of many of the victims of the telephone tapping in question." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then it goes on at paragraph 46 to say this: "The Court further considers that it is necessary to take the greatest care in assessing the need, in a democratic society, to punish journalists for using information obtained through a breach of the secrecy of an investigation, or a breach of professional confidence, when those journalists are contributing to a public debate of such importance and are thereby playing their role as 'watch-dogs' of democracy." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't quite see where it is. Is it paragraph 47?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Paragraph 46, the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: 46, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then if you look at paragraph 48, the Court considers what it called the admittedly fairly moderate fine that was imposed on the applicants, and the chilling effect that an interference with the freedom of expression could have on the exercise of freedom. And then at paragraph 49, it concludes as follows: "In conclusion, the Court considers that the judgement against the applicant constituted a disproportionate interference with their right to freedom of expression and that it was, therefore, not necessary in a democratic society." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps I'll ask you the same question again. Would that be an example, among others, of what you understand the principle of proportionality to mean and how it's being applied by courts and tribunals around at least Europe or the Council of Europe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a clear-cut case, especially for paragraph 48. It shows that we risk self-censorship if there are too many limitations or if it is disproportionate compared to the actions. Self-censorship of journalists, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to turn to another document that you were shown a while ago, just shortly, by my friend the Prosecutor. It's under tab 79 of the Defence binder yesterday. Perhaps I don't have to show you the document, to expedite things. It's the joint declaration of the UN special rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression, the OSCE representative, and freedom of the media. And Mr. MacFarlane was good enough to read two of the principles that are stated in this document, and he asked you questions about possible exception to reporting on ongoing legal proceedings. And you confirmed or you said that those two exceptions were fair trial of an accused and presumption of innocence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the document before me, but I remember that it was the case. But I did not know of the nature of this document. I don't know whether it was a press release or whether it was a document published before a relevant body.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: May I ask you to focus on the -- it's the first bullet point at the top of the page that you have in front of you, and if I can just give you a few seconds to read it. Just the first bullet point on the top of this page.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: “No restrictions”, does it start with those words?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall indicating to my colleague earlier that in conformity with what this principle state, there's two recognised type of restriction to the freedom of expression in this context, and that's, one, the fair situation, fair trial for the accused, or a situation where the presumption of innocence of an accused is at stake? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even pointed out as long as the proceedings are not finished, this was the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall adding also that one of the situation in which proceedings come to an end is where the accused dies? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are three courses; a sentence that is final, statutes of limitations, or death.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And were you aware of the fact that at the time when Ms. Hartmann published her book and article which formed the basis of these proceedings, the accused, in relation to which decisions were rendered, had died? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that Mr. Milosevic had died? Well, yes, I think that we all got to know that a few minutes after he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And are you aware that by an order of the 14th of March of 2006, the Tribunal issued an order terminating the proceedings in the Milosevic case? Are you aware of that order?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This was a consequence of his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you just to comment briefly. You were shown another document by the Prosecution. Your Honour, it's under tab 80, 8-0, of the binder. It's the council of your recommendation of 10 July 2003. And I don't think I need to show you the document unless you need it. I will simply read two -- I'm grateful to the Registry. Thank you very much. I will simply ask you, Mr. Joinet, to focus on the first page of this document, and I'll ask you first to look at what I believe to be the fourth paragraph in that document, and I will read them to you. It says this: "Recalling that the media have the right to inform the public, due to the right of the public to receive information, including information on matters of public concern under Article 10 of the Convention and that they have a professional duty to do so." Can you --

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I do not have the paragraph in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can't find this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it should be under tab, we believe, 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, tab 79, fourth paragraph, talks of condemning.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It should be under tab 80, and you should have -- it should be under tab -- well, Your Honour, we have a different document. I'll just put the proposition, since Your Honour don't have it in front of you, and I'll put it for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, this is a Council of Europe recommendation, 2003/13, of the Committee of Ministers to member states on the provision of information through the media in relation to criminal proceedings, and it's dated the 10 of July of 2003. It's the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe. And forget for a moment the text, Mr. Joinet. I will read out to you two passages from that, and I will ask for your opinion on those. The first statement says this: "Recalling that the media have the right to inform the public, due to the right of the public to receive information, including information --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So sorry, Mr. Mettraux. Judge Guney wants to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you read this out, could you give us the reference again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The reference is a recommendation Rec, R-e-c, (2003) 13, 1-3, of the Committee of Ministers to member states on the provision of information through the media in relation to criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you tell us the tab where to find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We believe that -- we believe, Your Honour, that the -- we believe that the wrong document was placed in the binder, Your Honour, by our mistake, obviously. I will just read the statement. It's the declaration that was put in the binder, and this is the recommendation that relates to the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Joinet, in this document, the Council of Europe, the Committee of Ministers, says this: "Recalling that the media have the right to inform the public, due to the right of the public to receive information, including information on matters of public concern under Article 10 of the Convention, and that they have a professional duty to do so." Now, let me ask you this: Is this statement of principle by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe consistent with the position of the subcommission at the time when you worked for that body?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The right to receive is always linked to the obligation to 21 provide information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then there's the second and last passage that I want to read to you. It's two paragraphs down. It says this: "Stressing the importance of the media reporting in informing the public on criminal proceedings, making the deterrent function of criminal law visible, as well as in ensuring public scrutiny of the functioning of the criminal justice system." Again, Mr. Joinet, I have the same question for you. Is this position of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe consistent with the position of the Subcommission of the United Nations on Human Rights at the time when you worked for that body?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS JOINET [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the end of the questions in re-examination. There is only two issues outstanding, and we will propose to follow the same course than with the previous witness. And I think we've agreed with Mr. MacFarlane that as far as documents are concerned that have been shown to this witness, he has no objection to their being tendered from the Bar table, so we will do that in due course. And the same process has been agreed upon as far as questions are concerned from the amicus. I'm grateful to you, Mr. Joinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much for coming to testify at the Tribunal in this matter for Mr. Mettraux. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You are now excused, you may stand down, and please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will call our next witness, Your Honour. It's Ms. Natasa Kandic. And we may also indicate to the Chamber, as we have informed VWS, the Registry, and our colleague from the Prosecution, we will not call the third-and-last witness that was listed up to this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the court usher calling the witness or is he taking the previous witness out? And where is the witness being called from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't speak French. I will speak in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Kandic. My name is Guenal Mettraux. I'm appearing on behalf of Ms. Hartmann. Before we start, may I ensure that you're receiving translation in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please state your name and date of birth for the transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Natasa Kandic. 16th December 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you tell what is your current professional occupation?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: My occupation is in the field of human rights, especially various projects dedicated to the establishment of transition justice in the states of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in that context, are you heading or directing any particular body or centre?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am the founder and the director of the Humanitarian Law Centre, an organisation which documents war crimes and deals with transition justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And briefly, because there are many, but in your capacity as founder and director of this centre, and for your various activities for human rights, are you the recipient of any prize or awards?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received various awards, the last one two days ago. It was the award of a local organisation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I won't go into the detail of those, but have you, for instance, been listed by "Time" magazine as one of the heroes of 2003, and one of the past 60 years, of 2007? Is that an accolade that you received?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honours, simply for the record, the curriculum vitae or at least a part of it is available under tab 82 of the binder, and we won't -- there's no need, I believe, to go any further into the detail of that. We will tender this.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, is your centre, the Humanitarian Law Centre, in any way related to this Tribunal, its mandate, or any of its organs?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- in fact, I was the first person, the first human rights activist, from the states of the former Yugoslavia that the OTP invited in August 1994 to help them in gathering relevant information, as they were only beginning their work on the first investigations at the time. And just after that, a few months later, perhaps, we at the Humanitarian Law Centre arranged, prepared, and translated into English very valuable documentation concerning massive violations of human rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And on many occasions later, we submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor our own documentation and shared with them our contacts with the witnesses. We helped in providing the witnesses and finding witnesses, and we maintained very, very close cooperation in our primary field of activity, which is the documentation of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't mind, Mr. Mettraux, just one little question. When was the Humanitarian Law Centre founded, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In November 2002 -- sorry, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kandic. Can you tell whether your organisation, the Humanitarian Law Centre, also took any step to make the work of this Tribunal and its proceeding better known in the region, that is, in the countries that form the former Yugoslavia? Have you taken any such steps?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We organised four large conferences where we presented the judgements of the Tribunal in The Hague, precisely because we believed it was very important to promote the judicial truth as established by formal judgements. We organised gatherings, always attended by more than 150 participants, about judgements in the Brcko case, the Srebrenica case, the Foca case, the Celebici case; and those were the only conferences in Serbia where the evidence underlying the judgements was discussed in great detail. And we invited, also, the witnesses to share with us their point of view on the establishment of judicial truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And could you explain, perhaps shortly, why it's important for your centre to participate in this outreach effort of the work of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Because the Humanitarian Law Centre, as well as other human rights organisations, supported vigorously the work of this Tribunal because this was the first such international institution to stop violence and war crimes by starting war crimes trials, and after that, nobody could count on impunity. We believed that our cooperation with the ICTY, and primarily with the Office of the Prosecutor, was important precisely in terms of resisting the culture of impunity which had been dominant for years in all the states of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me turn for a second -- we'll come back to some of those issues in a moment, but let me now turn back to something different, your relationship with Ms. Hartmann, the accused in this case. Can you recall approximately where and when you first met Ms. Hartmann, and, if so, in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Back in the 1990s, Florence Hartmann was a very well-known journalist in the states of the former Yugoslavia, especially after the outbreak of armed conflicts. She was recognised as a journalist who was everywhere where human rights were being violated and as someone who was reporting in a very objective and truthful manner. In those years, in 1991 and 1992, we were only beginning to deal with human rights, and we learned about violations of human rights for the first time, on many occasions, from the reports of Florence Hartmann. I remember very well the time when she was thrown out of Serbia, she had to leave the country, and that was the time when human rights organisations and I, personally, reacted very violently against that. But it was a time also when the voices of human rights activists did not matter at all, and Florence Hartmann and other important and good journalists had to leave Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Just following up on what you said of Ms. Hartmann being thrown out of Serbia, do you know who threw out Ms. Hartmann from Serbia and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: She had to leave Serbia pursuant to the decision of the authorities. At that time, the authorities were, in fact, a whole system headed by Slobodan Milosevic, but I believe that particular decision was taken by the Ministry of the Interior. She had to leave the country because of her alleged biased reporting and allegedly creating a climate of intimidation for many in Serbia. In other words, she was just doing her job professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you know what the real reasons for Ms. Hartmann to be thrown out of the country by Mr. Milosevic were?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, but it was my impression, and that impression was shared by many, namely, that the problem was that Ms. Hartmann travelled from Belgrade to Vukovar, and thanks to her reporting, we received some information about what was going on in Croatia, in Vukovar, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Kozarac, in and other places where in 1991 and early 1992 grave war crimes were committed. That is the perception we have in human rights organisation, that that was the main reason; namely, to stop the flow of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And after the war ended in the former Yugoslavia, have you continued to see and entertain relations with Ms. Hartmann?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: I always followed her work, and she visited frequently, mostly in Bosnia and Herzegovina. She was the kind of journalist who was very attached to the region of the former Yugoslavia. She's a great connoisseur of the region, and later she became the spokesperson for the Office of the Prosecutor. And for me and for all the other human rights activists, it was important, because we believed it was good for a person like that to occupy the position of spokesperson, a person who had great knowledge, a person who had been in countless locations and places of grave war crimes, a person who does not need additional education about what had happened. She had direct experience in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is Ms. Hartmann in any way related to the Humanitarian Law Centre that you're heading?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Last year, in 2008, we elected a new board of management, and since she was no longer working with the ICTY, it seemed to me that it was a good opportunity to approach her and invite her to become a member of the board of management of the Humanitarian Law Centre, because it would have been contrary to the rules of the Humanitarian Law Centre to do it while she was the spokesperson of the ICTY. As she was now a freelancer, I invited her. And beginning with 2008, she is a member of our board.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And was her reputation, whether professional or personal, to the extent you can testify to either of those, of relevance to your decision to invite her to become a member of the board?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I have known Florence Hartmann since the 1990s. She's a journalist, a reporter, from whom I learned a lot. When I started working on war crimes in 1991, it was extremely important to me to know which journalists were objective, which journalists actually travel and eye-witnessed war crimes, whose information I can take as a reliable starting point in our investigations and inquiries. In all these years, it never happened that something Florence Hartmann wrote turned out to be untrue or objectionable in any professional sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And when you learnt of the indictment before this Tribunal of Ms. Hartmann for an alleged contempt of court, did you consider taking her off the board, did you consider that you should do so, the board of the centre?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation was bizarre. I did not learn about this indictment from her, and that did not really surprise me, because I've known her for years and she's not that kind of person. She's not the kind of person who would discuss her own problems or say that something is hard for her or difficult. I read about it in the newspapers. Her first reaction, when she eventually called me up, was to ask if it was all right for her to continue to be a member of the executive board of the Humanitarian Law Centre. I was taken aback by the question and even a little offended. I wondered, could she possibly be thinking that the most important thing for me, when deciding to invite her to become a member of the board, was that she had been a spokesperson of the OTP, but that was, in fact -- that arose, in fact, out of her both human and professional subtlety. She was prepared to go to great lengths to avoid any embarrassment to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the usher please assist and give the binder that is here to the witness. Thank you very much. Your Honours, this is binder number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, could I ask you, please, to turn to what is tab 83 of this binder, number 83.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you, Ms. Kandic, a press release from the Humanitarian Law Centre, dated the 3rd of November, 2008, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you have any part in preparing this document, Ms. Kandic? And if so, what part?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I participated in drafting this document, together with other listed organisations that are the signatories of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And let me read, perhaps quickly, the first paragraph of that document. It says this: "Concerning the trial of Florence Hartmann conducted before The Hague Tribunal for the alleged publication of confidential Appeals Chamber decisions in the Slobodan Milosevic case, human rights organisations from the successor states to the former Yugoslavia would like to draw attention to the fact that the content of these decisions was the subject of many press reports and public debates after the International Court of Justice delivered its judgement in February 2007 in the case BiH versus Serbia on charges of genocide, and it is not clear why Ms. Hartmann has been singled out by The Hague Judges." Now, you indicate in that paragraph that there were many press report and public debate. Can you tell, in very general terms, what those related to?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. All of us, I and other human rights activists, were astonished by the indictment because we discussed the contents of these controversial decisions for years before that, especially intensively during the establishment of the International Court of Justice, because it was common knowledge that these transcripts and records of the Supreme Defence Council exist and certain sections of these transcripts were redacted. It was a constant topic, what these transcripts were about, what was hidden in them, and there was no opposition by the authorities to what we, the human rights organisations, were saying; namely, that those transcripts contained those parts of the debates and deliberations on the Supreme Defence Council that concerned Srebrenica, primarily, and the involvement of the police and army forces of Serbia in those events. I spoke about it openly. Nobody ever said, This is not true, that's not what these redacted parts of the transcripts contain. Nobody ever called into question, back in our country, that the Government of Serbia applied to the Tribunal in The Hague for this decision to protect these redacted parts of the transcript for that reason. What was at issue was the contents of the transcripts. It seemed completely illogical to us that one person should be singled out for discussing it. I remember that this book by Florence Hartmann appeared in press reports after so many other discussions in the media. We didn't -- we couldn't understand why Florence Hartmann was being singled out, because we were discussing openly these things in the press. There was even an expert seminar in our region that was organised after the judgement of the International Court of Justice in June and July 2007. We couldn't understand the standard by which this one person was being singled out, while all of us were being allowed to debate the contents of the said decisions. That brought us activists in the field of human rights in a strange situation, and we were discussing the transparency of the proceedings in the Milosevic case and other cases, why such a decision to hide these parts was taken in the first place, and why this standard of national security was being applied in that way. We discussed this national security interests not only in Serbia, but in the whole region. We discussed it many times, and we always faced the same dilemma; whether the acceptance of this standard really contributed to establishing the facts of these events; whether it was really in conformity with the obligation of the Court to take into account all the relevant facts that could help us find out what really happened; why all these things could not be public. And we believed that there should be as little secrecy as possible, especially in war crimes trials. The ICTY was in a situation for the first time to help uncover the truth about what happened and why it happened, and we all expected from this Court to put it out in the public eye and to help us in the region gain knowledge of these facts and to start thinking about what happened in the past; and, with the benefit of these facts, to resist and defy the culture of impunity, and use these facts to establish personal liability and responsibility, but also the responsibility of the authorities and the state. And it seemed to us that this was an inadequate standard in the context of war crimes trials but also in trials aiming to establish the responsibility of states. It seemed to us completely inadequate from the viewpoint of human rights, and it did not tally with the way we thought courts should act in establishing personal responsibility and state responsibility. And I still believe that this criterion, this standard, should be widely debated and that lawyers' organisations and human rights organisations should be allowed to openly discuss this; namely, whether this standard is in keeping with the need to establish facts and to present them publicly in order - how shall I put it? - to create a different climate in the states that had been engulfed in the conflict. Also, we in the human rights organisations thought that the courts, whether criminal courts and criminal cases or the International Court of Justice, should be careful, when taking decisions, to be aware that if such decisions have to find a balance between national security and the need to find justice, there is a factor of the victims and their expectations. They expect courts to take decisions that will satisfy justice, and by taking a different kind of decisions, they help the states which are prepared to commit the most terrible crimes in their own interests. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, we will come to that in a moment. If you can just focus on the question. You've covered a lot of ground, but I'll ask you to try to answer the question as precisely as you can, since we have little time. But can you indicate to the Chamber whether the information that you have indicated you had, you, the Humanitarian Law Centre and other organisations, about the redaction that had been ordered on to the records of the SDC, did you get that information prior to the publication of Ms. Hartmann book or only after?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed. I, personally, and other human rights activists, had been aware of that information long before the book was published. It was a topic in the media, it was widely discussed in public. Representatives of the state of Serbia, even those who were in the Defence teams, said that the state had to be protected, that national security of the state is of the utmost importance, and they publicly advocated the importance of concealing some information. On the other hand, we felt that the establishment and the disclosure of facts was very important for the establishment of justice in the states of the former Yugoslavia. We felt that this was impermissible, and this was a topic that was present in public, at various meetings. It wasn't something we discovered when the book appeared. For us, the book did not discover anything new, and it wasn't something that we started discussing when the book appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Let me show you a few examples. Perhaps we will go a little bit faster on this. Can you look under tab 84 bis of your binder in front of you. Under that tab, you will find a "New York Times" article dated 9th of April, 2007, written by Marlise Simons, and it's called "Genocide Court Ruled for Serbia Without Seeing Full War Archives." Do you have that? Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you tell me, have you been interviewed for purposes of this article?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to the journalist of the "New York Times," and as you can see this was in April 2007, which by far preceded the publication of Florence Hartmann's book, and the topic was the transcripts and minutes of the supreme Defence Council. And I said much more on that occasion than appears in the text. I told the journalist to what extent --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, Ms. Kandic, just a second. I will come to the part that pertains to your interview. Let me take this article one step at a time. If you look at the first two paragraph, it discuss that in the spring of 2003, during the trial of Mr. Milosevic, hundreds of documents arrived at the Tribunal. Then it refers, in the next paragraph, to a cache of documents. And then in the third paragraph, it says that Serbia, the heir to Yugoslavia, obtained the Tribunal's permission to keep the parts of the archives out of the public eye. And it goes on to say: "Citing national security, its lawyers," that's Serbia's lawyers, "blacked out many sensitive - those who have seen them saying incriminating - pages ..." And then in the next paragraph, it refers to lawyers and others who were involved in Serbia's bid to secrecy. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you turn now to the next page of that article from "The New York Times" and look at a paragraph towards the end of the page, which starts with the words: "However, lawyer who have seen the documents ...," it's three paragraphs from the bottom. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what "The New York Times" journalist was saying in that piece is that: "Lawyers who have seen the archives and further secret personnel files say they address Serbia's control and direction even more directly, revealing in new and vivid detail how Belgrade financed and supplied the war in Bosnia, and how the Bosnian Serb Army, though officially separate after 1992, remained virtually an extension of the Yugoslav Army. They said the archives showed in verbatim records and summaries of the meetings that Serbian forces, including secret police, played a role in the take-over of Srebrenica and in the preparation of the massacre there." From what I've read to you, does it appear that the journalist of the "New York Times" in April of 2007 is discussing what she believes to be the content of the SDC minutes? Is that what there is in this passage?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: In this passage, yes, it does refer to the contents of those minutes. And I recall that talking to this journalist, though this is not stated here, I mentioned that in the case of the Skorpions, this is a case being tried before the national court for war crimes in Belgrade, that as a representative of the victim, I was able to get hold of many documents which confirm what the journalist says in this paragraph. There were documents signed by the minister of police of the Bosnian Serbs or, rather, Republika Srpska, from which it can be seen that in July 1995, during the Srebrenica operation, not only did members of the Skorpions take part, but also other members of the Serbian police force, so that for me this story as to whether Serbian regular forces, that is, from Serbia, from the Republic of Serbia, participated in this so-called Srebrenica operation did not provoke any dilemma at all in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, just a second. Let me ask you the questions, and try to focus on those. These discussions, such as the one I've just read to you from "The New York Times" article, were those matters that were also discussed in the public, generally, and/or among human rights organisations in the Balkan and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. In the media, in gatherings of human rights organisations, this was discussed quite openly. On the one hand, we had human rights organisations, who believed that the Government of Serbia must take a decision to disclose the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council and that this concealment of information and facts must be put an end to. And it was general knowledge that regular forces of Serbia had taken part in Srebrenica. On the other hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: One thing at a time. The next question, Ms. Kandic: Those public discussions that you've said took place, can you specify, did they take place before the publication of the book of Ms. Hartmann, after the publication of the book of Ms. Hartmann, or before and after? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: They started long before the publication of the book. They started -- I think the discussions over this topic appeared with greater frequency thanks to an inquiry by the London Institute for War Reporting, and it was then that this became a very important issue in the community of human rights organisations. We devoted a great deal of attention to this issue to demonstrate that there was absolutely no doubt in our minds as to the content of those documents, and that we demanded that they be disclosed; therefore, long before the publication of the book. But naturally from 2005, this has gone on to the present.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Let me show you another document. You've just referred to an inquiry by the London Institute for War Reporting, which is also known as IWPR. It's under tab 84 ter of your binder. I believe that's the next document. You should have an article from IWPR of the 17th of May of 2005, and it's entitled: "Special Investigation: Justice at What Price. Allowing Belgrade to keep key evidence from public view in the Milosevic trial could have grave repercussions for justice and reconciliation." Just briefly, can you say whether that's the article to which you refer?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the article I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then if I can just draw your attention to the first paragraph of that article, it says this: "The Hague Tribunal allowed Belgrade to present key documents in the long-running trial of Slobodan Milosevic on condition that they were kept under wraps, delivering a blow to those who want justice to be seen to be done." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can turn to the third page, please, of that document. And if you look at -- I think it's the fourth paragraph on that page, it starts with the words: "The document which ...," and I will read it out for the transcript. It says: "The documents which now enjoy protected status at the Tribunal are known to contain references to the regime's involvement in the Bosnian war. The most important papers recount the activities of the then Yugoslav state's highest political and military body, the Supreme Defence Council, SDC, from 1992 to 1999." And if you can now turn to the next page, please, you will see in the middle of the page or so there's a subtitle saying "Belgrade's Damage-Limitation Exercise." And then the first paragraph refers to Rule 54 bis of what is the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, and the article says or claims: "It is on the basis of this rule that the Belgrade government applied for protection of the full SDC archive, stating in a number of sessions held before Hague Tribunal Judges that publication would endanger the interests of Serbia and Montenegro." Did you have in your possession, and I mean by "you," your centre in particular, but the human rights community and the victim community in Serbia and elsewhere in the Balkan, did you have all that information available to you at the time and were you discussing it publicly?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This inquiry and this text dates back to May 2005, as I can recollect, and I also spoke to this investigator of the Institute for War Reporting, and this was a topic that was discussed within the human rights community. And it was then that we became fully conscious of what was happening and what Serbia had achieved as a result of such a ruling of the Appeals Chamber, in a situation when it is extremely difficult to establish the truth as to who participated and who is responsible for the events in Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if you go on reading the article, you will see there's a -- it says that the protective measures had been asked to protect Serbia in relation to the ICJ proceedings, and at the bottom of the page it says: "Answering the IWPR's question whether the ICJ case was the main reason why his government insisted on keeping the documents protected, the man then in overall charge of negotiations with the Tribunal, former Serbian and Montenegrin Foreign Minister Goran Svilanovic, answered 'absolutely correct.'" Let me ask you this. In your various contacts with Serbian officials, whether it be Mr. Svilanovic or anyone else, did they ever seek to hide the fact that they had, in fact, sold and obtained protective measures that we are discussing from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: No, this wasn't concealed at all. It was even praised. Everyone in Serbia -- or, rather, representatives of the authorities praised the strategy of the new authorities. And when there were criticisms from the human rights activists that, in this way, the state is protecting a criminal state led by Mr. Milosevic, the response from the official side was that the state has to be protected, even Milosevic's state. But I repeat, it was not concealed at all. It was known that the main reason was the forthcoming proceedings in the International Court of Justice and the need for Serbia to be protected from documents being presented in the court which would show that Srebrenica was carried out with the direct participation of regular formations from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps to save a bit of time, I also draw your attention to page 7 of this article, which may be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, if I can ask you to go to the last page of that document, please. There should be a statement that has been attributed to you. If you look, it starts with the words: "Natasa Kandic," and I will read it out to you. It says: "Natasa Kandic, director of the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade, links this kind of denial to the government's refusal to be open about the past." And then there is a quote attributed to you. It says: "In this case, the government thought that the national interest was to prevent Bosnia from using documents in its ICJ case by hiding the truth." Then there's another quote attributed to you. It says this: "But the real national interest is in creating a healthy society in which the Milosevic regime's role in the war is widely known and accepted. This will not happen if important state documents continue to be hidden from public view." Could you explain briefly what you intended to convey with that statement?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: I think that everything is quite clear here. What I believe is that when the government of Serbia requests a certain document or parts of documents could be -- should be protected from the public eye by the tribunal passing such a decision, that this is contrary to the most important demands and requirements of every society after wars, and that is for the society to learn the truth, and that is the only guarantee that such things would not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You indicated a moment ago that Serbia and then Serbia-Montenegro never sought to hide the fact that they had sought and obtained protective measures from this Tribunal in relation to the SDC records. Did they ever try to hide the fact that these decisions granting the measurements were, for some of them, confidential?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: But this was not an issue. No one from the authorities of Serbia mentioned that those decisions were confidential. It was only after the discussion that we organised in June 2007, after the judgement was passed, that is, on the 29th of June, 2007, only then, as the panel included representatives from the Serbian team, Professor Rade Stojanovic and Sasa Obradovic, only then did this lawyer, Sasa Obradovic, mention that those decisions were confidential. On the other hand, the head of the Defence team, Professor Rade Stojanovic, said that he was in favour of the contents of the minutes being disclosed and that he had said that several times. So the main issue was never that the court rulings were confidential, but the discussions always centered on the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And by "content," what do you mean? What content or contents?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: I mean the contents, that is, the facts that everyone knew related to the facts and evidence on the involvement of the police and Army of the Republic of Serbia in the perpetration of the genocide in Srebrenica. Of course, the best evidence of this was when, at this panel meeting held in June 2007, the leader of Serbia's Defence team said that they had done everything, including obtaining protective measures for certain documents, so as to defend Serbia from the accusations that it had participated in genocide. It was so clear that those documents -- or, rather, the request and obtaining of protective measures, that this had helped Serbia's team to defend Serbia from the charges, and that was the main reason for the request for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps just to save time again, Ms. Kandic, can you confirm that this conference, which you've indicated you organised -- and, Your Honour, the excerpt from the record of this conference are available under tab 85 bis. Can you tell me, Ms. Kandic, whether during that conference the representative of Serbia - I think you mentioned Mr. Sasa Obradovic and Professor Stojanovic and former ambassador for Serbia and Montenegro - whether they formally discussed during that conference the existence of these confidential orders granting protective orders to the SDC minutes and the fact that these ordered had been granted by this Tribunal? Can you just confirm that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, they spoke about this quite frankly and openly because it was a topic that was widely discussed, and they couldn't just get up and say they knew nothing about it. This was something discussed publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Just so we don't have to spend too much time on the document, the Judges and the Prosecutor have this document in front of them, could you say -- we have a record of this conference, and everyone in the courtroom has a copy of it. Could you confirm, is that a verbatim transcript of the discussion that took place during this conference?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I also have a book. It is the transcript of the entire discussion, word by word.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is this document public?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The book has been published, and all the participants and members of the panel have a copy, as do many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you ever receive a complaint that the content of that document inaccurately reflected what any of the participants had said during that conference?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll simply refer to tab 85 bis, and we'll tender it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, can you turn, please, to tab 86 of your binder. Ms. Kandic, as you will see, this is an excerpt from the public -- from a public hearing before the International Court of Justice. It's dated the 8th of May, 2006, and the passage that you have is at -- starts at page 27, and it is an answer to the question posed by one of the Judges of the ICJ, Judge Simma. And the person speaking is the representative of Serbia and Montenegro in the case that opposed it to Bosnia and Herzegovina. At paragraph 55, Ms. Kandic, the representative of Serbia says this: "Madam President, allow me now to turn to another issue - the question posed by Judge Simma in relation to the blackened sections of the documents of the Supreme Defence Council of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then just if you continue down the text, in paragraph 56 you will see there's a reference to a letter of the agent of Serbia and Montenegro, dated 16 January, and then you will see, again in the last sentence of that paragraph, the representative of Serbia refers to, I quote: " ... the contents of the redacted parts of the minutes and stenographic notes of the supreme command of our state." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's the last sentence of paragraph 56. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We'll come back to this page, but if you can turn for a second to the next page, at paragraph 59, please. And in the opening sentence, you will see that he says: "Madam President, with all due respect to this Honourable Court, the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro are not entitled to discuss," and I quote again, "the contents of the redacted sections of the Supreme Defence Council documents at this moment ..." Just interfering a question there, in your view, and perhaps you've said it before, but what was the -- what were the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro to seek to maintain under confidentiality? Was it the contents of the SDC minutes, or was it the existence of decisions in relation to these documents, or anything else?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: I've already said they were protecting the contents. They didn't want the facts and data to be presented which we, from the human rights organisations, publicly expressed doubts as to the contents of those documents, that this related to the involvement and the engagement of the Serbian police and army in the perpetration of the genocide in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll simply refer to the rest of the transcript at a later stage. Could we move into a private session for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps with the assistance of the usher, there is a document which we would like distributed and, please, not put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: 20th of April, 2006, record of the ICJ proceedings between Serbia and Bosnia. And if you turn the page, you'll see at page 40 it's the representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina who is addressing the Court, and he's talking about the Supreme Defence Council and the reports thereof or the records thereof. And if you turn at page 41, he's goes on about the same subject. And at page 42, paragraph 43, the representative of Bosnia says the following: "Only recently - actually in the midst of the pleadings that took place here before this Court - it," and that would be Serbia and Montenegro, "tried to make sure that the ICTY would not make public its confidential decision ordering Serbia and Montenegro to produce certain documents, including Ratko Mladic's personnel file." Now, I'd like to focus at this stage solely on Mr. Mladic's personnel file. Is that issue or the fact -- the fact that there were resistance on the part of the Serbian government to produce the personnel file of Mr. Mladic, known at the time of this proceedings in April of 2006, was it in the public domain?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: The public in Serbia was aware that there was a standing request of The Hague Tribunal for the personnel file of Ratko Mladic to be produced, but in the media you could hear and read representations by the Serbian authorities that such a file does not exist, that it can't be located, nobody knows where it was, and it was quite clear to the public that Serbia did not wish to turn over that file, that it contained information that Serbia did not want disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps to accelerate things, we'll do two things. First, we'll refer to a decision from the Milosevic prosecution case, in any case, dated the 16th of June, 2005. And it's called: "Decision on Prosecution's motion to admit into evidence Ratko Mladic's Yugoslav Army (VJ) personnel certificate." And Your Honour will see that there's a very open and public discussion in that document of that fact. But, Ms. Kandic, we'll go back to tab 84 ter for a second, if I may. Could the Registry assist? 84 ter, and it should be page -- Ms. Kandic, page 14 of that document. Unfortunately, there's no number in the version that we've printed, but it would be five pages from the end of the document. So if you can work backwards, it's the fifth page from the end, and there is a subheading called "Selective Memory?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you slow down, please. It becomes very difficult to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you have it, Ms. Kandic?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It says this: It's the IWPR article, just for the record's sake, IWPR article of 17th May, 2005. It says this: "There are indication that some other --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. The document is not paginated, so we --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We need to get to --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is five pages from the end, Your Honour, and there is a subheading almost in the middle of the page saying "Selective Memory?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The what page from the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you count five pages from the end, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this is tab 84?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Tab 84, Your Honour, ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, I will read it out to you, to expedite things. It says this: "There are indications that some other relevant documents have not been made available and some may have gone missing. One such document appears to suggest that, like his RS Army officer corps, General Mladic, himself, received a salary as if he were a regular member of the Yugoslav military. The Serbian and Montenegrin foreign minister's legal counsel chairman, Professor Radoslav Stojanovic, revealed to IWPR in August of 2004 the existence of a secret Yugoslav Army order from 1993 awarding Mladic a promotion. It was signed by then Yugoslav president, Zoran Lilic, in his capacity as chairman of the SDC." And if you can turn, please, to the next page, at the top of the next page, the piece goes on to say: "Although the promotion order was leaked to media in Sarajevo media in November 2004, it does not seem to have been sent to the Tribunal under the protective measures deal. "IWPR has obtained a copy of Mladic's personnel file which includes pension information and the dates of promotion orders. The documents show that Mladic received his final promotion on June 16, 1994, to the rank of colonel-general. His personnel file substantiates Professor Stojanovic's statement that Mladic remained an officer in the Yugoslav Army long after Belgrade said he was no longer under its command." And I simply have a very, very short question, Ms. Kandic, in relation to that, is: Were these facts as stated in the article of May 2005, were they well known in the public, and in particular within victims and human rights organisations in Serbia and elsewhere in the Balkan?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: We all knew that there had been a 30th Personnel Centre, as it was called, and that it was through this centre that the salaries of all the officers of the Army of Yugoslavia, which later was renamed the Army of Serbia-Montenegro, were paid out, and that applied to all those who were assigned to stay on in Bosnia after the 19th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Just a second. We need to, unfortunately because of time restraint, we need to go very fast. Can you tell me whether the information that I've read out to you from the article was widely or publicly available in the public and, in particular, within victims and human rights organisations in Serbia prior to the publication of Ms. Hartmann book? Can you confirm that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was known. We all knew, also, of this report by the Institute for War Reporting, and we in the human rights organisations were aware of that. As for the public, it was quite normal to the public in Serbia. Everyone knew that Ratko Mladic was an officer of the Yugoslav Army and that the Army of Republika Srpska was part of that Army of Serbia-Montenegro, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There was no dilemma about it. Everybody knew that there would be no Army of Republika Srpska without the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I've done all of my questions, and tried to do as fast as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Any cross-examination, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm directing your attention to the conference in Belgrade on the 29th of June, 2007, which is tab 85 bis in the Defence materials. You've already referred to that, and you've made reference to various comments that were made, and in particular comments concerning whether certain materials should remain confidential or whether it should be released. And on my review of the transcript of this conference, it appears to be somewhat in the nature of a debate. And I direct your attention to -- the portion I'm wanting to direct your attention to apparently is not included in the Defence materials, although I expect it will be in your book, which contains the transcript of the proceedings at page 93 and 94, a statement by Sasa Obradovic, that's O-b-r-a-d-o-v-i-c. And what that person said was this: "You only fail to tell us how you obtain this document. I shan't go into this issue here, but it's as simple as that if you come by a document which has been protected from public eye by The Hague Tribunal, then you are committing an offence of disrespecting the Tribunal, you know. Some journalists from Croatia have answered for something like this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- before you give the answer, you talked of -- what you are reading coming from your book. I'm not quite sure which book are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have that document with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The Defence filed a part of the proceedings at the seminar, and this is not included in the Defence materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would have no objection, if it expedites things, that we tender the entire transcript, if that cuts short the issue, and if Mr. MacFarlane can address that in final submission, we would have no objection to it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course, if Mr. MacFarlane has to refer to part of that document that has been tendered, yes, the rest must be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that passage from Sasa Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It would appear that that person was clear that protected materials need to remain protected, and that you're committing an offence if it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a very -- in our submission, a very unfair way to put the question. If Mr. MacFarlane wishes to put that proposition, I think he has to refer to what was being discussed before, which was the content of the redacted document themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you can deal with that in re-examination. Mr. MacFarlane, you are reading from the minutes of this conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And is it not true that Sasa Obradovic is with the Embassy of Serbia in the Netherlands and is noted as being with the Embassy of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true, he's a civil servant. But this is the only place in this entire conference that one of the civil servants of Serbia mentions the decision on confidentiality or the confidential decision. And for the benefit of the Judges, you say "you only fail to tell," that's the way you quoted it, so the Judges might think that Sasa Obradovic was addressing me. You should say that he was addressing a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I take it from the fact that different views were being presented at this seminar, that it was a seminar of different perspectives and different views.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. On the one hand, there were representatives of the Defence team of Serbia participating. They held one position. On the other hand, we had representatives of human rights organisations who kept repeating their position that all protected documents should be available to the public. And then some other representatives were victims from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their position, too, was that the state of Serbia was duty-bound, for the sake of the past and for the sake of the victims, to disclose the documents. And also, of course, there were representatives of the Defence team of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who thought that in this way, Serbia prevented the Serbian public from knowing in which way the genocide in Srebrenica had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that this seminar essentially was a series of views being expressed by individuals, and they were not intended to be a description of the official position of the Government of Serbia, but rather were the views of individuals.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC
utterances.text: But, please, the representatives of the legal team of Serbia could not state their private opinions there. They are civil servants. They represented the state as a legal team, and they always, always stated the positions in keeping with the entire legal strategy of defence. The only exception at that panel meeting, and in all these years up to the present, was Professor Stojanovic, who said that he was in favour of disclosing all the protected documents. But no one else from that team took it up or supported it, and even he never said something like that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are, in essence, two further areas. I'm very much alive to the time, and there are two quite important areas. I will endeavour to deal with them as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. Obviously, if you haven't finished, we'll have to postpone, and the witness will have to come back again. There's still re-examination to take place. There might be questions from the Bench also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In respect of the final two areas that I intended to deal with, at least today, it will be necessary to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kandic, unfortunately we have not been able to finish with you. You will have to come back and testify to finish your testimony. And just to warn you that while you are away from court during the period of postponement, you are not supposed to discuss this case with anybody until you finish testifying. Okay? Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, unfortunately, availability is very difficult in the very near future. This matter is going to have to stand adjourned to the 1st of July, 2009. I guess the parties will be advised of the courtroom and the time, but it will be the 1st of July. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of July, 2009. 21 22 23 24 25
